subject: Critical Thinking
title: The Representativeness Heuristic: Judging by Stereotype
description: A quick, practical guide to The Representativeness Heuristic: Judging by Stereotype.

hook.text: Linda is 31, outspoken, philosophy major. Is she more likely a bank teller, or a bank teller who is a feminist?

buildup.text: Representativeness: judging probability by how much something resembles a stereotype, ignoring actual frequency.

discovery.text: The 'Linda problem' proves we substitute similarity for probability.

twist.text: We do this constantly: a well-dressed man must be a CEO, a quiet kid must be shy.

climax.text: Representativeness ignores base rates. There are far more bank tellers than feminist bank tellers.

punchline.text: Looking like something doesn't make it likely. Count the actual numbers.

quiz.question: Why do people fall for the Linda problem?
options: They substitute similarity to a stereotype for actual probability

details.summary: The representativeness heuristic judges probability by how closely something matches a mental prototype. A quiet, book-loving person seems more likely to be a librarian than a salesperson, even though salespeople vastly outnumber librarians.
details.whyItMatters: This heuristic causes you to ignore base rates and make probability judgments based on stereotypes, leading to systematic errors in a wide range of decisions.
takeaways: We judge likelihood by resemblance to a prototype
Base rates are ignored when a vivid description is available
The conjunction fallacy is a direct result of representativeness

faq.question: What is the conjunction fallacy and how does it relate to representativeness?
faq.answer: The conjunction fallacy occurs when people judge a specific combination as more probable than one of its components alone. Linda the feminist bank teller seems more likely than Linda the bank teller because the description fits a feminist prototype.

faq.question: How can you counteract the representativeness heuristic in practice?
faq.answer: Always ask about the base rate before evaluating how well a description fits. If 99% of people in a pool are salespeople, even a bookish introvert is more likely to be a salesperson than a librarian.
